paper_title: Demystifying the Autoresearch Harness: How Context and Skills Shape Self-Evolving Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Autoresearch agents, which autonomously design, run, and refine experiments, are accelerating scientific progress, particularly in AI research. However, existing agents rely on harnesses that combine multiple mechanisms, making it difficult to determine how individual components contribute to performance. We systematically study harness design for long-horizon, self-evolving autoresearch agents along two dimensions: context management, which determines what an agent retains from its past attempts, and skill management, which governs how it stores and reuses lessons from those attempts. Across MLE-Bench and KernelBench with gpt-oss-120b, gpt-6-luna, and gpt-6-sol, we isolate the effects of individual harness design choices by evaluating each against a recency-truncation baseline within a shared agent framework. For context management, we find that preserving individually accessible records of past attempts is more effective than maintaining a rolling summary, with context folding performing best across all six settings and improving upon the baseline by up to 19.2%. For skill management, selectively discarding persistently unused lessons is more effective on average than consolidating them or promoting them to standing rules. Building on these findings, we combine context folding and skill deletion in MLEvolver, which achieves a 72.7% medal rate on MLE-Bench Lite and a 94% $\mathrm{fast}_1$ score on KernelBench Level 3, substantially outperforming AIDE and OpenEvolve under the same inference budget. Overall, our study distills design principles for preserving experimental history and curating reusable lessons in autoresearch harnesses, paving the way for agents that turn accumulated experience into sustained progress.

However, existing agents rely on harnesses that combine multiple mechanisms, making it difficult to determine how individual components contribute to performance. Introduction Autoresearch agents can automate the cycle at the heart of empirical research: given task and grader, they propose an idea, implement it, run the experiment, read the result, and decide what to try next. They are becoming increasingly important in AI for AI (AI4AI), where improving existing AI systems directly accelerates subsequent research. Recent autoresearch agents demonstrate this across diverse domains: on MLE-Bench [Chan et al., 2025], AIDE [Jiang et al., 2025], and ML-Master [Liu et al., 2025b] iteratively train and tune competitive machine learning pipelines. On KernelBench [Ouyang et al., 2025], Kevin [Baronio et al., 2026] learns to write and iteratively refine fast CUDA kernels, and AlphaEvolve [Novikov et al., 2025] has even sped up the training of the language models it is built on. What is common among these workflows is their long horizons operation. The agent attempts the same task tens or hundreds of times, receives an evaluation score after each attempt, and iteratively refines its solution. Over such horizons, an agents behavior depends not only on its language model, but also on the harness that manages the memory it accumulates about its own past. This memory takes two forms, each under different kind of pressure. The first is the history of past attempts. It grows with every attempt, and soon exceeds the context window, thereby leading to truncation [Packer et al., 2023].

sections.content: Figure 1 We evaluate contextand skill-management mechanisms for long-horizon AI autoresearch on Kaggle competitions in MLE-Bench and CUDA kernel optimization tasks in KernelBench. MLEvolver combines context folding and skill deletion, the strongest mechanisms in their respective dimensions. MLEvolver outperforms AIDE and OpenEvolve on both benchmarks, achieving 72.7% medal rate across 22 MLE-Bench Lite competitions and 94% on fast1 across 50 KernelBench Level 3 problems. The second is library of skills: natural language lessons distilled from earlier attempts and retrieved when similar situation recurs [Shinn et al., 2023, Zhao et al., 2024]. The library can grow without limit, but it can become redundant and noisy, which makes the right lessons harder to retrieve. What an agent keeps, condenses, or discards in each form of memory is therefore central design decision. Many mechanisms have been proposed for managing this memory. Agents page information in and out of context [Packer et al., 2023], reflect on and summarize past experience [Park et al., 2023, Shinn et al., 2023], and extract, revise, and reuse insights or workflows [Zhao et al., 2024]. However, these mechanisms are typically evaluated within multi-component systems where differences in search policies, prompt structure, and tool use confound cross-system comparisons. Even when individual studies ablate their own designs, memory mechanisms are rarely evaluated head-to-head under shared, unified harness. As result, it remains unclear what each mechanism contributes on its own. We address these questions through controlled, bottom-up study of memory harness design in iterative self-improvement, where an autoresearch agent repeatedly attempts the same task and receives empirical feedback after each attempt. This setting strains both memory tiers early: the execution history quickly overflows the context window, while the skill library accumulates redundant lessons. Starting from minimal recency-truncation baseline, we isolate five memory mechanisms within an otherwise identical agent by changing exactly one component at time (Figure 2). Two manage working context: folding condenses each attempt into an expandable digest, and compaction aggregates older history into running summary. Three govern the skill library: deletion prunes unused lessons, merging consolidates semantic duplicates, and promotion elevates proven skills into persistent standing rules. Our contributions are as follows: controlled study of harness design for long-horizon, self-evolving autoresearch agents: six configurations within one agent that isolate five contextand skill-management mechanisms against recency-truncation baseline. An evaluation across three model backbones and two AI4AI benchmarks, with analyses of the effectiveness of per-attempt digests in folding, the dual benefits of skill retention and active management, and differences in skill retrieval behavior across backbones. MLEvolver, harness that combines context folding and skill deletion and substantially outperforms AIDE and OpenEvolve on MLE-Bench Lite and KernelBench Level 3. 2. Related Work Harness Design and Memory in Autoresearch. Autoresearch harnesses orchestrate iterative discovery by structuring how language models store, retrieve, and build upon past attempts. Existing systems couple search logic with bespoke memory stores: FunSearch [Romera-Paredes et al., 2024] and AlphaEvolve [Novikov et al., 2025] maintain program databases, AIDE [Jiang et al., 2025] manages candidate trees, and ML-Master [Liu et al., 2025b] integrates selectively scoped execution log into its harness. Broader agent harnesses also develop targeted mechanisms to mitigate context bounds. These harnesses page state in and out of prompt buffers [Packer et al., 2023], summarize completed sub-goals [Hu et al., 2025], train models to fold execution trajectories [Sun et al., 2026, Ye et al., 2026], or mask older observations to match summarization at reduced token cost [Lindenbauer et al., 2025]. For procedural skills, prior frameworks accumulate verbal reflections [Shinn et al., 2023], distilled insights [Zhao et al., 2024], or synthesized experience replays [Liu et al., 2025a]. However, uncurated skill catalogs degrade retrieval accuracy as they expand [Li, 2026]. Recent harnesses address this bloat through heuristic forgetting [Zhong et al., 2024], pruning low-utility records [Xiong et al., 2026], or injecting curated operational playbooks into working context [Chen et al., 2024, Zhang et al., 2026]. Unlike prior frameworks designed for single trajectories, cross-task transfer, or brief retries, autoresearch harnesses must sustain refinement across long horizons of scored attempts. In our study, we compare five contextand skill-management mechanisms within shared harness, varying one component at time. AI4AI Benchmarks. growing set of benchmarks employs agents to automate the development of AI systems themselves, direction that ML-Master [Liu et al., 2025b], MLAgentBench [Huang et al., 2024] and MLE-Bench [Chan et al., 2025] task agents with improving machine learning models on research problems and Kaggle competitions. KernelBench [Ouyang et al., 2025] and TritonBench [Li et al., 2025] focus on writing correct and fast GPU kernels. On RE-Bench [Wijk et al., 2025], agents outperform human experts under short time budgets but gain less from longer ones, so the effectiveness of making use of long run of attempts remains an open problem for autoresearch agents. We use MLE-Bench and KernelBench, where every attempt is scored, so each mechanisms effect can be tracked throughout run.

sections.content: 4. Experiments 4.1. Experimental Setup We evaluate the five memory mechanisms and baseline on two machine learning benchmarks. MLE-Bench evaluates agents on Kaggle machine-learning competitions [Chan et al., 2025], while KernelBench evaluates agents ability to generate fast and correct GPU kernels for machine-learning workloads [Ouyang et al., 2025]. We use three model backbones, gpt-oss-120b [OpenAI et al., 2025], gpt-6-luna [OpenAI, 2026a] and gpt-6-sol [OpenAI, 2026b]. For merging, Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B [Zhang et al., 2025] is used to generate the skill embeddings. Each task has an independent skill library, which is reset before the task begins. All configurations for given task start from the same seed solution that is curated to be deliberately weak. The memory policy determines how the attempt history and skill information occupy the context. MLE-Bench. We evaluate on 10 competitions from MLE-Bench [Chan et al., 2025], comprising six low-complexity and four medium-complexity competitions. The selected competitions and benchmarkspecific modifications are detailed in Appendix B. Each configuration runs 100 iterations per competition. In each iteration, the agents solution trains on the competitions training data and writes submission, which is then graded. The agent then receives its score under the competitions metric, together with any terminal output produced during execution. Because the metrics differ in scale and direction, we report gold-normalized score (GNS), analogous to the human-normalized score in reinforcement learning [Mnih et al., 2015]: GNS𝑖 = 100 𝑠𝑖 𝑠0 𝑖 𝑠gold 𝑠0 𝑖 𝑖 , (7) the score of do-nothing submission, and 𝑠gold where 𝑠𝑖 is runs best score on competition 𝑖, 𝑠0 𝑖 the gold medal threshold on MLE-Benchs leaderboard for that competition [Chan et al., 2025]. We aggregate over the 𝑁 = 10 competitions with weights 𝑤𝑖 of 1 and 2 for lowand medium-complexity competitions: 𝑖 GNS = (cid:205)𝑁 𝑖=1 𝑤𝑖 GNS𝑖 (cid:205)𝑁 𝑖=1 𝑤𝑖 . (8) KernelBench. We evaluate 50 KernelBench problems across three difficulty levels [Ouyang et al., 2025]: 20 Level-1 individual operators, 20 Level-2 fused operator chains, and 10 Level-3 model architectures. Appendix A.2 describes how the evaluation subset is constructed. Each configuration runs for 50 refinement iterations per problem. At each iteration, the generated CUDA kernel is compiled and evaluated against the PyTorch Eager reference implementation on randomly generated inputs. The evaluation runner applies static and runtime safeguards against reward hacking, including checks for prohibited code patterns and protection against reusing reference outputs. Implementations that violate these checks are invalidated. Appendix A.1 describes the correctness and timing procedures, while Appendix A.3 details the reward-hacking safeguards. We report the geometric-mean speedup over PyTorch Eager, consistent with recent evaluations of agent-generated GPU kernels [Dai et al., 2026, Younesian et al., 2026]. The geometric mean provides continuous summary of multiplicative performance gains across the 50 tasks and is less sensitive than the arithmetic mean to exceptionally large speedups.

How Context Affects Agent Performance We quantify how often an attempt advances the incumbent solution using the new-best rate: the share of attempts whose score beats every earlier attempt of the same run. We report it for the first 10% of the iterations and for the rest. Figure 3 Context usage and progress under different context-management mechanisms. (a) Average number of past attempts and average context tokens in the coders prompt. (b) New-best rate for the three mechanisms. The three context management mechanisms achieve similar new-best rates during the first 10% of iterations. As shown in Figure 3b, folding reaches 35.4%, compared with 36.3% for compaction and 35.3% for the baseline. After the first 10% of iterations, when more past attempts have accumulated, folding achieves the highest average new-best rate at 12.0%, compared with 10.2% for the baseline and 9.7% for compaction. Folding therefore discovers improvements about 18% more frequently than the baseline and 24% more frequently than compaction during this later stage. Figure 3a shows how folding expands access to experimental history. The baseline retains an average of 6.2 recent attempts in full and discards earlier history. In contrast, folding condenses each attempt into compact digest of the attempted strategy and its outcome, retaining records of 42.0 past attempts on average while allowing the agent to recover full records when needed. It achieves this broader coverage with approximately 12.1k context tokens on average, compared with 18.4k for the baseline. Access to these prior successes and failures allows the agent to target each new attempt more effectively. Compaction also uses approximately 12.1k tokens on average, but it achieves lower later-stage new-best rate. It merges all older attempts into one summary of bounded length, which cannot keep pace with growing history. Together, these results indicate that reducing context usage alone is insufficient to sustain improvement. The representation must also preserve useful access to accumulated experimental history.

sections.content: 5.2. Separating Skill-Library and Management Gains To separate the benefit of maintaining skill library from the additional benefits of managing it, we compare each mechanism with No-Skill ablation in which the skill writer and picker are disabled. Figure 4a reports relative performance changes computed separately for each modelbenchmark setting and then averaged across settings. Figure 4 Performance and skill retrieval under different skill-management mechanisms. (a) Gains over the no-skill agent. Each mechanism adds its management gain (solid segment) to the baselines library gain (hatched segment). (b) Skills picked per prompt (bars, left axis) and gain over the same models baseline (dots, right axis), averaged across both benchmarks. (c) Share of offensive and defensive skills among the selected skills, averaged over MLE-Bench and KernelBench. Introducing an unmanaged skill library improves average performance by 2.1% over No-Skill, showing that recording and retrieving lessons benefits iterative refinement. Managing those lessons provides further gains over the unmanaged baseline, with deletion yielding the largest average improvement at 4.1%, followed by promotion at 3.0% and merging at 2.2%. Deletion uses the model backbones recent skill selections as signal of relevance, pruning persistently unselected lessons as the run progresses. This also reduces the number of entries the picker must consider. As shown in Figure 8, on MLE-Bench with gpt-oss-120b, deletion leaves 31 skills at the end of the run, compared with 312 for the unmanaged baseline and 330 for promotion. Merging and promotion use different criteria, which explains their smaller average gains. Merging consolidates semantically similar skills, but can weaken specific applicability conditions or implementation details. Promotion keeps lessons from earlier attempts as standing rules, even when the solution evolves and their original conditions no longer apply. Appendix E.3 illustrates these issues with case studies from both benchmarks. 5.3. Model Differences in Skill Retrieval and Orientation The different gains from skill management coincide with differences in how the three model backbones use the skill library. Figure 4b shows that gpt-oss-120b retrieves 6.47.1 skills per prompt across configurations, whereas gpt-6-luna retrieves 1.21.9 and gpt-6-sol retrieves 0.50.6. This ordering holds across the baseline and all three skill-management mechanisms, suggesting consistent differences in the models skill selection behavior. The models also differ in the orientation of the knowledge drawn from the skill library. We classify skill as offensive when it encourages new implementation, optimization, or search direction intended

sections.content: to improve the score, and as defensive when it primarily protects the current solution by preserving correctness or avoiding known failures. Full classification criteria are provided in Appendix E.1. As shown in Figure 4c, 53.1% of the skills retrieved by gpt-oss-120b are offensive, compared with 30.2% for gpt-6-luna and 25.4% for gpt-6-sol. Together, these observations suggest that the two proprietary backbones, gpt-6-luna and gpt-6-sol, use the skill library more conservatively. They draw on fewer stored experiences and more often select knowledge aimed at protecting existing performance. The open-weight backbone, gpt-oss-120b, draws on broader set of experiences with more even balance between protective guidance and active optimization. This difference offers one explanation for why skill management provides larger gains for gpt-oss-120b. 6. MLEvolver: Combining the Best Choice in Each Dimension Context folding and skill deletion deliver the largest average gains among the context-management and skill-management mechanisms, respectively. We combine them in MLEvolver and compare the resulting harness with AIDE and OpenEvolve on 22 competitions in MLE-Bench Lite and 50 problems in KernelBench Level 3. We track how each system improves over 100 iterations and compare its final performance. Figure 5 Performance of MLEvolver, AIDE, and OpenEvolve. (a) Any-medal and gold-medal rates across the 22 MLE-Bench Lite competitions. (b) fast1 and fast2 across the 50 KernelBench Level 3 problems. (c) Gold-normalized score on MLE-Bench Lite through 100 iterations. (d) Geometric-mean speedup over PyTorch Eager on KernelBench Level 3 through 100 iterations. 6.1. Setup Harnesses. MLEvolver combines the best-performing mechanism on average in each dimension: folding for context management and deletion for skill management. AIDE [Jiang et al., 2025] searches

sections.content: a tree of candidate solutions. At each step, it drafts new solution, refines the best node found so far, or debugs failing node. OpenEvolve [Sharma, 2025], an open-source implementation of AlphaEvolve [Novikov et al., 2025], maintains program database organized into islands. At each iteration, it samples parent program and provides high-performing and inspiration programs as context. The model edits the parent using search-and-replace diffs. Benchmarks and budget. We evaluate 22 competitions in MLE-Bench Lite, the low-complexity split of MLE-Bench [Chan et al., 2025], and 50 problems in KernelBench Level 3, which covers full model architectures [Ouyang et al., 2025]. All three harnesses use gpt-6-sol, 32K-token context window, and budget of 100 iterations per run. Metrics. We track progress over iterations using the gold-normalized score (GNS) on MLE-Bench Lite and geometric-mean speedup over PyTorch Eager on KernelBench, as in Section 4. We also report any-medal and gold-medal rates on MLE-Bench Lite, the percentages of competitions in which the best submission reaches at least the bronze and gold thresholds, respectively [Chan et al., 2025]. On KernelBench, we report fast1 and fast2, the percentages of problems with correct kernel whose speedup over PyTorch Eager exceeds 1 and 2, respectively [Ouyang et al., 2025]. 6.2. Results MLEvolver outperforms AIDE and OpenEvolve on both benchmarks. As illustrated in Figure 5a and Figure 5b, MLEvolver earns medals in 16 of 22 MLE-Bench Lite competitions (72.7%), relative gain of 23.1% over AIDE and 14.3% over OpenEvolve. It wins 10 gold medals, 42.9% more than either baseline. On KernelBench Level 3, MLEvolver reaches 94% on fast1, relative gain of 20.5% over AIDE and 34.3% over OpenEvolve. At the stricter fast2 threshold, MLEvolver produces correct kernels with more than 2 speedup over PyTorch Eager on 31 of 50 problems (62%), more than twice as many as AIDE and more than four times as many as OpenEvolve. These results show that MLEvolver is effective for long-horizon, self-evolving autoresearch on machine learning tasks. MLEvolver pulls ahead early and extends its lead. Figure 5c and Figure 5d show that MLEvolver reaches 97.4 GNS by iteration 20 on MLE-Bench Lite and 2.08 geometric-mean speedup by iteration 10 on KernelBench Level 3. On both benchmarks, these early results exceed the performance that AIDE and OpenEvolve reach at iteration 100. On MLE-Bench Lite, MLEvolver maintains its lead and finishes at 98.1 GNS, 1.4% higher than AIDE and 2.6% higher than OpenEvolve. On KernelBench, MLEvolver widens its lead in the second half of the run. Between iterations 50 and 100, its geometric-mean speedup increases by 11.9%, from 2.67 to 2.99, while AIDE and OpenEvolve improve by 0.8% and 5.2%, respectively. 6.3. Discussion Folded history supports informed exploration and refinement. All three systems can explore different approaches. AIDE [Jiang et al., 2025] follows predefined policy for drafting, debugging, and improving solutions, with hyperparameters controlling the number of initial drafts and debugging behavior. OpenEvolve [Sharma, 2025] samples parent and inspiration programs from its populations according to configured rules. In MLEvolver, the model uses catalog of attempt digests to decide whether to refine promising solution, debug failure, or propose new approach when progress stalls. It can also retrieve full records of relevant earlier attempts, including their code, recorded reasoning, scores, and execution output. This combination provides an overview of previously explored directions and access to the details needed to build on earlier successes and failures. The value of retaining this access is reflected in Section 5.1, where folding preserves more experimental history within the context window and achieves higher new-best rate during later iterations.

sections.title: Demystifying the Autoresearch Harness
sections.content: Distilled skills give MLEvolver direct guidance for later attempts. AIDE summarizes earlier valid solutions, and OpenEvolve provides selected programs alongside summaries of recent changes, metrics, and outcomes. Alongside the attempt digests, MLEvolver maintains separate library of lessons distilled from its experiments. Retrieving these lessons directly reduces the need to reconstruct them from earlier code and results. Offensive skills suggest promising directions to explore, while defensive skills record constraints and failure patterns that can help the model avoid repeating mistakes. Deletion prunes persistently unselected skills, using the models retrieval behavior as signal of which lessons remain relevant as the search progresses. The benefits of both retaining and managing these lessons are supported by Section 5.2, where maintaining the skill library improves performance and deletion provides further gain. Solution space shapes scaling. The two benchmarks differ in the structure of their solution spaces. On MLE-Bench Lite, the solution space is more discrete, with promising solutions built around distinct choices of model family and feature representation. The harnesses can therefore start with substantially different submissions, contributing to the spread in GNS at iteration 1. On KernelBench, the solution space is more continuous. The first correct kernels run about as fast as PyTorch Eager on average, and later optimizations yield incremental speedups. These differences favor different search strategies. On MLE-Bench Lite, exploring several distinct candidates increases the chance of finding strong solution. AIDE explores candidates across branches of search tree, and OpenEvolve samples from population of programs. As the runs progress, AIDEs gap to MLEvolver narrows from 3.5% to 1.4%, and OpenEvolves narrows from 15.4% to 2.6%. On KernelBench, successive optimizations can build on one another, favoring sequential self-refinement. MLEvolver uses single refinement chain with context folding and skill deletion, so each new edit can draw on results and lessons from earlier attempts. AIDE refines node in its search tree, and OpenEvolve edits sampled parent with guidance from selected programs. In both cases, the model has more limited view of which optimizations succeeded or failed in earlier attempts. Between iterations 50 and 100, MLEvolver increases its geometric-mean speedup from 2.67 to 2.99, while AIDE and OpenEvolve make smaller gains and finish at 1.85 and 1.41, respectively. 7. Conclusion We present controlled study of harness design for long-horizon, self-evolving autoresearch agents. Within one agent, we isolate five memory mechanisms and compare each with recency-truncation baseline on MLE-Bench and KernelBench using gpt-oss-120b, gpt-6-luna, and gpt-6-sol. Three findings emerge from the experiment. First, folding performs best in all settings by condensing each attempt into short digest, allowing the agent to retain more experimental history within the context budget and target solutions more effectively. Second, both retaining skills and actively managing them improve performance, with deletion providing the largest average gain among skill-management mechanisms. Third, the benefits of skill management vary with the model backbones skill selection behavior. Both gpt-6-luna and gpt-6-sol retrieve fewer skills and favor defensive guidance more strongly than gpt-oss-120b, accompanying their smaller gains from skill management. Based on these findings, we combine folding and deletion in MLEvolver, which achieves 72.7% medal rate on MLE-Bench Lite and 94% on fast1 on KernelBench Level 3, outperforming AIDE and OpenEvolve on both benchmarks. Overall, our study identifies effective choices for preserving experimental history and curating reusable lessons, providing an empirically grounded foundation for long-horizon, self-evolving AI research agents.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Our study isolates memory mechanisms within linear, sequential refinement loops and leaves parallel scaling unexplored. Parallel search strategies, such as concurrent tree search and population-based evolution, distribute attempts across parallel trajectories and place distinct demands on context budgets and skill selection. Our system comparisons cover structured autoresearch frameworks with guided research loops. Interactive coding agents, such as Claude Code or Codex, are not evaluated. They execute open-ended sequences of tool calls and internal refinement rounds, making it difficult to define common unit of iteration or enforce comparable evaluation budgets across systems. Finally, each task initializes an independent skill library. Our findings therefore characterize within-task experience accumulation, leaving other evolutionary effects, such as cross-domain skill transfer and multi-task skill distillation, for future work.

sections.content: A. KernelBench Protocol and Evaluation Details We evaluate all agent configurations on 50 tasks from KernelBench [Ouyang et al., 2025]. This section describes the evaluation environment, timing procedure, task subset selection, and reward-hacking safeguards. A.1. Evaluation Environment and Timing Protocol All evaluations execute on dedicated NVIDIA GH200 144G HBM3e GPU. The software environment runs Python 3.10.20, PyTorch 2.11.0+cu128, and CUDA 12.8. Equivalence Verification. Following Ouyang et al. [2025], functional correctness evaluates numerical output equivalence between the PyTorch reference implementation and the agents submitted kernel on identical input tensors. Latency Measurement. The original KernelBench protocol [Ouyang et al., 2025] uses the arithmetic mean execution time across runs to compute speedup, as its benchmark suite exhibits coefficient of variation (𝜎/𝜇) below 3%. In our long-horizon agent setting, execution times do not consistently remain within this variation threshold across repeated compilation and execution passes. We therefore use the median execution time to compute speedup, reducing the influence of transient operatingsystem overhead and driver allocation spikes. A.2. Stratified Problem Selection KernelBench contains 250 problems across three difficulty levels. The full suite includes many similar operations evaluated with different tensor shapes, so uniform sampling could overrepresent some computational patterns. We therefore construct 50-task subset from 28 strata defined by computational structure. The subset includes at least one task from every stratum and preserves the benchmarks 2:2:1 level distribution: 20 Level-1 tasks testing individual operators, 20 Level-2 tasks testing fused operator chains, and 10 Level-3 tasks testing model architectures. Table 2 lists the selected problems and their stratum assignments. Sampling Frame and Exclusions. Our sampling frame contains 238 of the 250 KernelBench problems: 99 from Level 1, 89 from Level 2, and all 50 from Level 3. We exclude 12 problems for the following reasons: Degenerate problems (3 Level-2 tasks: p23, p80, and p83). The reference implementations produce outputs that are either identically zero or numerically indistinguishable from zero under the benchmarks correctness tolerance. For example, in problem 80, column-wise maximum reduces the tensor to single column, after which mean subtraction and GELU produce an all-zero output. trivial kernel that returns zeros can therefore pass numerical validation without performing the intended computation. We exclude these problems because they do not meaningfully evaluate kernel optimization. Algebraically reducible problems (8 Level-2 tasks: p13, p14, p18, p42, p44, p51, p65, and p98). In these problems, matrix multiplication or convolution is followed by operations that permit most of the original computation to be removed through algebraic simplification. For example, the reference computation in problem 14, (cid:205) 𝑗 (𝑥𝑊) 𝑗/2 𝑠, can be rewritten as (cid:16)(cid:205) 𝑗 𝑊𝑗 /2 𝑠. This reformulation replaces general matrix multiplication (GEMM) with less 𝑥 expensive general matrix-vector multiplication (GEMV). We exclude these problems because their performance is determined primarily by discovering an algebraic shortcut. (cid:17) Missing reference timing (1 Level-1 task: p95). sections.content: We determine the initial number of tasks assigned to each stratum using regularized form of Neyman allocation [Neyman, 1934]: 𝑛ℎ = 𝑛 𝑁ℎˆ𝜎ℎ 𝑘=1 𝑁𝑘 ˆ𝜎𝑘 (cid:205)𝐻 , (9) where 𝐻 = 28 is the number of strata, 𝑛 = 50 is the total sample size, 𝑁ℎ is the number of eligible tasks in stratum ℎ, and 𝑛ℎ is the number sampled from that stratum. The quantity ˆ𝜎ℎ estimates the within-stratum standard deviation of log(speedup) across pilot replicates. We regularize this estimate toward an analytic optimization-headroom score ranging from 0 to 3. We also require every stratum to contain at least one sampled task. The level budgets are fixed at 20, 20, and 10 tasks, matching the full benchmarks 2:2:1 distribution. Sampling weights account for this difference when estimating performance over the eligible frame. Subset Selection and Runtime Matching. Using the stratum allocations, we generate 3,000 candidate subsets by sampling uniformly without replacement within each stratum, with seed 20260919. We select the candidate that best matches the 238-task sampling frame in log reference runtime, using an objective that combines the KolmogorovSmirnov (KS) distance, the difference in mean log runtime, and deviation from the target level distribution. Reference runtime is the median latency of the PyTorch eager implementation on the evaluation hardware and is independent of agent performance. A.3. Anti-Reward-Hacking Safeguards Kernel-generation agents can discover shortcuts that increase measured speedup without implementing the intended computation [Baronio et al., 2026, Dai et al., 2026]. We combine static code inspection, runtime isolation, and prompt-based guidance to detect or discourage these strategies. Reference Output Isolation. Prior work has shown that candidate kernels may exploit outputs left in GPU memory by the preceding reference execution [Baronio et al., 2026]. In particular, candidate that allocates an uninitialized tensor may receive memory containing values from the reference output and pass numerical verification without writing every output element. We prevent this shortcut by retaining the reference output until numerical verification is complete, so its device memory cannot be reused during candidate execution. Static Code Inspection. Before compilation, we inspect each candidate implementation using Pythons ast module. The validation gate rejects candidates that: 1. do not define explicit CUDA source containing at least one __global__ kernel; 2. delegate all reference operations to high-level frameworks or compilation interfaces instead of implementing complete operation in custom kernel; 3. patch timing functions, reference modules, or evaluation code; 4. modify input tensors or tensor references in place; or 5. spawn background threads or processes, or defer timed work to an execution stream that is not synchronized with the primary stream. candidate that fails any of these checks is marked invalid and can never become the tasks best attempt; speedup is computed from each tasks best valid attempt. Numerical State Isolation. Candidates also attempt to alter the evaluation by changing process-wide numerical settings, such as PyTorch matrix-multiplication precision or global TF32 flags. The harness records the relevant numerical settings and restores the required evaluation configuration before reference timing. Candidates that modify prohibited precision or backend settings are rejected. This

sections.content: prevents candidate from obtaining an apparent speedup by reducing numerical precision or by slowing the reference implementation. Prompt-Based Integrity Guidance. The runtime safeguards are complemented by prompt instructions that discourage invalid optimization strategies before code is generated or reusable knowledge is recorded. These instructions guide the agent toward genuine kernel optimization but are not treated as enforcement mechanisms. KernelBench Integrity Rules 1. Compute the intended operation. At least one custom CUDA kernel must implement complete operation or fused group from the reference model. Dummy kernels, identity operations, and staging copies do not qualify. 2. Preserve correctness beyond observed inputs. Implementations may specialize to the declared shapes, dtypes, constructor arguments, and target GPU, but not to particular input values, weights, memory addresses, call counts, or random seeds. 3. Use only exact simplifications. Algebraic rewrites are allowed when they preserve the reference computation for every valid input and weight. Approximations and shortcuts that hold only for observed test inputs are not allowed. 4. Preserve the required numerical precision. Implementations may not introduce lower-precision arithmetic, approximate mathematical operations, or prohibited changes to process-wide precision settings. 5. Do not manipulate evaluation. Implementations may not modify inputs, reference buffers, timers, backend settings, execution streams, threads, or processes to influence correctness or latency measurements. B.
